title: Chapter 24: Humidity, Saturation, Clouds and Precipitation

blocks.content: Water vapour is the most dynamic component of the atmosphere. Although it forms only a small fraction of atmospheric gases, it controls weather processes, cloud formation, rainfall, heat balance, and human comfort.
1. What is Humidity?

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: Oceans supply nearly 86% of atmospheric moisture through evaporation.
Warm air holds significantly more water vapour than cold air, influencing regional humidity capacity.
Saturation occurs when air reaches 100% relative humidity, initiating condensation at the dew point temperature.
Condensation requires air cooling and the presence of condensation nuclei like dust, smoke, or salt particles.
Cloud seeding uses silver iodide to induce rainfall, while virga refers to rain evaporating before reaching the ground.

blocks.content: Humidity refers to the amount of water vapour present in the air at a given time. Water vapour enters the atmosphere mainly through evaporation from oceans, rivers, lakes, and soil, and through transpiration from plants.
• Warm air can hold more water vapour than cold air.
• Humidity is highest in equatorial regions and lowest in deserts and polar areas.
• Oceans supply nearly 86% of atmospheric moisture.
• Humidity strongly influences temperature because water vapour absorbs terrestrial radiation.
2. Types of Humidity (Conceptual Understanding)
To understand atmospheric moisture scientifically, humidity is measured in multiple ways. Each type answers a different meteorological question.

cells: The actual mass of water vapour present in one cubic meter of air (g/m³). It tells us how much moisture physically exists in the air but changes with air volume.
Ratio of water vapour mass to total air mass. It remains nearly constant even when air expands, making it very useful in meteorology.
The percentage of moisture present compared to the maximum moisture the air can hold at that temperature. It indicates how close the air is to saturation.
Also called moisture-holding capacity. It is the maximum amount of water vapour air can hold at a given temperature. Higher temperature → greater capacity.

blocks.content: 3. Everyday Examples to Understand Humidity
• Clothes dry faster in summer because warm air has higher humidity capacity and can absorb more moisture.
• Clothes dry slowly during the monsoon since the air is already near saturation.
• Desert coolers work efficiently in dry regions because low humidity allows rapid evaporation.
• Earthen pots (matkas) keep water cool due to evaporative cooling — water seeps through tiny pores, evaporates, and removes heat.
• We feel uncomfortable in coastal cities because high humidity prevents sweat from evaporating.
• Winter air feels dry because cold air has low moisture capacity.
4. Humidity Capacity and Saturation
Saturation occurs when air holds the maximum amount of water vapour possible at a given temperature. At this stage, relative humidity becomes 100%.
Water vapour is the most dynamic component of the atmosphere.
• When air cools, its moisture-holding capacity decreases.
• Once the dew point temperature is reached, condensation begins.
• Further cooling leads to formation of droplets, fog, or clouds.
• Any additional moisture results in precipitation.
Dew Point – The Key Concept
The dew point is the temperature at which air becomes fully saturated. A high dew point indicates humid conditions, while a low dew point suggests dry air.
5. Measurement of Humidity
• Hygrometer – measures atmospheric humidity.
• Psychrometer – uses wet and dry bulb thermometers.
• Dew-point hygrometer – directly determines saturation temperature.

Low capacity to hold water vapour
Faster drying due to higher moisture capacity
Slow drying due to near saturation or low capacity

blocks.content: 6. Condensation – From Invisible Vapour to Visible Droplets
Condensation is the process through which water vapour transforms into liquid when air becomes saturated.
• Requires cooling of air.
• Needs condensation nuclei such as dust, salt particles, or smoke.
• Adiabatic cooling (rising air) is the most important mechanism.
Forms of Condensation

cells: Water droplets deposited on cool surfaces overnight.
Ice crystals formed when temperature falls below freezing.
Dense cloud at ground level reducing visibility below 1 km.

blocks.content: 7. Clouds – Formation and Atmospheric Role
Clouds form when rising air cools adiabatically and reaches saturation. They regulate Earth’s temperature by reflecting solar radiation during the day and trapping heat at night.
8. Precipitation – Final Stage of Atmospheric Moisture
Precipitation occurs when cloud droplets combine and become heavy enough to fall under gravity.

cells: Large ice balls formed in strong updrafts.

items: Orographic rainfall creates dry rain shadow regions on the leeward sides of mountains.
Dew point is the critical threshold temperature at which air becomes fully saturated.
Silver iodide is used as a nucleating agent in cloud seeding operations.

blocks.content: Types of Rainfall
9. Advanced Concepts
• Latent heat released during condensation fuels storms.
• Rain shadow regions develop on leeward mountain sides.
• Virga is rainfall that evaporates before reaching ground.
• Cloud seeding uses silver iodide to induce rainfall.
MASTER EXAM REVISION POINTS

• Warm air holds more moisture.
• Relative humidity indicates saturation level.
• Dew point marks condensation temperature.
• Cumulonimbus clouds cause thunderstorms.
• Orographic rainfall creates rain shadow deserts.
